newsitem.title: UK: Analysts detect first nerves over Glaxo.
newsitem.headline: Analysts detect first nerves over Glaxo.

text.p: Shares in Britain's Glaxo Wellcome Plc slipped back on Thursday as analysts detected the first sign of market nerves over the imminent demise of ulcer drug Zantac and herpes treatment Zovirax.
Although the company produced interim results in the middle of market forecasts, shares fell by up to 44-1/2 pence before recovering to trade down 27-1/2 pence at 13.02 stg late Thursday afternoon.

"I think people have been expecting some volatility to come into the picture on the Zantac patent expiry. The sheer scale of the numbers is just starting to hit home," said Daiwa analyst Nigel Keegan.

CS First Boston analyst Genghis Lloyd-Harris said the prospect of two years of flat-to-declining sales and operating margins as Zantac retreated stood out in a sector where people were focused on growth.
"People have focused on the long-term because the stock has gone up a long way (this year), but at some point it feels fairly valued and we think it is at that point now," he said.
And Dresdner Kleinwort Benson analyst Peter McDougall added that "anybody who has got Glaxo shares has got to be assuming that the market is prepared to live with that miserable outlook."
The group's shaving down of profit margin forecasts for the full-year to 35.0 percent, compared with 37.5 percent achieved in 1996, underlined the harder road ahead.

After achieving first-half margins of 38.5 percent, finance director John Coombe told analysts he expected margins to slip to the low 30s in the second half of this year and the first half of next, before recovering in the second half of 1998.
But as the company replaces the blockbuster sellers Zantac and Zovirax with a package of newer drugs, Dresdner Kleinwort's McDougall said "margins will never get back to these levels."

"You cannot make as much profit out of 10 little drugs as you can make out of two big ones. If you look at large drug companies they have all made it on the back of blockbusters, where you can get economies of scale and profits," he added.
McDougall said the 13 pound valuation on the shares would be hard to justify at lower margins, with ten or eleven pounds more realistic.
Daiwa's Keegan however said even at lower levels, Glaxo's margins were ahead of most of its competitors.

"If people were buying before these results they should still be buying now," he said. "They are a very well-managed company with some good products and they are a good long-term investment. But I wouldn't be buying them to make a profit in three to six months."
And BZW analyst Steve Plag said: "Glaxo is set to become one of the strongest drug companies in the world by 1999. The key message is that sales ex-Zantac were up a stunning 14 percent."

Analysts said there had been good news for Glaxo in the form of a delay to the entry of generic competitors in the U.S. market, where Zantac's patent expired last week. A flurry of lawsuits among would-be suppliers has given Glaxo and its daily $5 million sales of Zantac a free run until the end of August at the earliest.
Keegan said the gap added a penny to the group's full-year earnings per share, while a further delay until the end of September could add another two to three pence.
"Any suspicion of further delays will be good news," he said.
